title: #15 Use the hypothesis and critical evidence combo when coaching
author: Craig Barton
summary: Barton turns the weekly tip on the adults for once, describing the change that took his own instructional coaching from what he calls wishy-washy at best to something colleagues actually buy into. The method is a pairing he names the hypothesis and critical evidence combo. He spends the first few minutes of a lesson observation simply watching teacher and students to form a hypothesis - that students have not understood an explanation, that the teacher will miss something visible from the observer's seat, or that something is about to happen. He then spends the following minutes deliberately gathering evidence for that specific hypothesis: counts of students not doing something, a direct quote of the teacher's words, a student's answer to a question he asked them, or photographs of work. In the coaching conversation the hypothesis comes after specific praise, and the evidence comes immediately after the hypothesis. His argument for why this works is the contrast with the vague alternative he used to offer - 'I am not sure all students were engaged' - which gives a colleague nothing to accept or act on. The evidence lends credence to the hypothesis and gives coach and teacher a shared, quasi-objective basis for planning next steps together.
points: The sequencing is the insight: hypothesis first, then evidence gathered specifically to test it, rather than recording everything and reasoning backwards at the end.
Barton is explicit that the observer's seat gives privileged information the teacher cannot have, which is what makes a hypothesis worth forming in the first place.

The evidence types he names are deliberately concrete and countable - a tally, a verbatim teacher quote, a student's answer to the observer, a photograph of work - because buy-in depends on it being checkable.
His diagnosis of why most coaching fails is that vague engagement claims give a colleague nothing to accept or dispute, so nothing can be built on them.
Praise comes before the hypothesis in his conversation structure, and the evidence immediately after it, which he treats as the key move rather than an optional courtesy.
quotes: Recently I have been lucky enough to do some coaching of maths colleagues in a number of schools that I work with. In the past my coaching has been wishy-washy at best, and pretty pathetic at worst.

Fortunately I have been able to learn from those far better than me, and I now have a coaching process that seems much more effective. I will share the process below, together with some examples of it in action, but first I wanted to mention what I consider to be the key change: the hypothesis, critical evidence combo.

When I first go into a lesson, I spend the first few minutes watching the teacher, watching the students, trying to get a sense of what is going on. Then I form a hypothesis. I may suspect students have not understood what the teacher has said, or that the teacher will not pick up on something that I can see from my privileged position, or that something is about to happen.

I will then spend the next few minutes gathering critical evidence to support my hypothesis. This could be something quantifiable (e.g. the number of students not doing something), a direct quote of what the teacher said, how a student responded to a question I asked them, or photos of students’ work.

In the coaching session, following specific praise on what the teacher did really well, I can present my hypothesis and then - and this is the key bit - share the evidence I gathered to support it. I cannot tell you how much more effective this part of the coaching process is in terms of getting a colleague to buy into it, compared to the usual vague "I am not sure all students were engaged" rubbish that I used to spout.
